questions.prompt: What is the MTU of standard Ethernet?
questions.explanation: Standard Ethernet has a 1500-byte MTU — the largest payload a single frame can carry on the link.

questions.prompt: In which header do port numbers live?
questions.explanation: Ports are a transport-layer concept, carried in the TCP/UDP header. The IP header has addresses, TTL, and a protocol field, but no ports.

questions.prompt: The IP header field that is decremented by each router and drops the packet at 0 is the ____ (IPv6 calls it Hop Limit).
questions.explanation: The TTL (Time To Live) is a hop counter that prevents packets from looping forever; traceroute exploits it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about fragmentation and MSS are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: IPv6 routers never fragment in transit; they drop and send 'Packet Too Big'
MSS is roughly the MTU minus the IP and TCP headers
IPv4 routers may fragment an oversized packet in transit
Fragmentation is preferred because losing one fragment is harmless

questions.explanation: IPv6 doesn't fragment in transit, IPv4 may, and MSS ≈ MTU − IP − TCP. Fragmentation is actually fragile: losing one fragment loses the whole packet.

questions.prompt: Order these from the innermost payload to the outermost wrapper for an HTTP request over TCP/IP on Ethernet.
questions.explanation: Encapsulation nests the HTTP data inside a TCP segment, inside an IP packet, inside an Ethernet frame.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The data a layer is carrying
Largest frame payload a link allows
Largest application-data chunk in a TCP segment
Splitting an oversized IP packet to fit the MTU

questions.explanation: Payload is the carried data; MTU limits frame size; MSS is TCP's data chunk derived from MTU; fragmentation splits packets that don't fit.
